newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - RBA cuts official interest rates.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - RBA cuts official interest rates.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Friday cut official cash interest rates by 0.5 percentage points to 5.5 percent, the fourth rate cut in the current cycle.
Rates were last cut by 0.5 percentage points to 6.0 percent in December 1996.
The following is a selection of economists' initial reaction to the announcement.

"I am surprised that they have done this. I would have expected no change until early 1998 when I would have expected rates to go up on the basis of very rapid growth in the U.S., translating into rapid growth here and adding to inflation. I have two problems with the RBA's rationale as interest rates have a slower effect than I think they think and two, growth has more of an impact than I think they think."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"Following the wages data I am not surprised. The wages data cleared the way and the Fed left a window of opportunity for the Reserve Bank not to have to cut through U.S. interest rates. And since there wasn't going to be any critical data between now and the next board meeting, it is not surprising that they have done it now. I think (the RBA's reasoning) stands up, I think it is fair enough."
HANS KUNNEN, GROUP ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"I am glad they did but given (RBA governor Ian) Macfarlane's earlier statements about wage growth, the inappropriateness of cutting interest rates -- he seems to have done a U-turn. So that is the level of my surprise, that he has gone completely against statements he made nearly a fortnight ago. I agree with the rate cut, I would have done it myself, but I didn't think they would. I thought they were more hawkish. I am not sure whose views have changed."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"(The RBA) has obviously taken a calculated risk that wages aren't a problem. They are also saying that underlying inflation is going to push below 2.0 percent, I think that's a pretty bold call. On top of that they also talking about the economy actually accelerating and are just giving it a bit of extra lift. Which ever way you cut it, this is a reasonably high risk interest rate cut."

"Well done Reserve Bank. I didn't expect they would react this quickly but I think it is very appropriate. Twenty-four hours ago before the wage numbers came out this would have been a surprise. I also think the (company) profit numbers reinforce the fact that this recovery is fragile and far from in the bag."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, J.P. MORGAN:

"It's a bit hard to make a case for this cut and I think the RBA's statement on the reasons was the weakest of the four so far. I know aggregate wage growth was revised back a little but private wage growth is a worry. Perhaps this was a reward for the IRC's restraint on the 'Living Wage' claim. The risk now is that with wages bottomed around four percent and the dollar -- which has helped so much in bringing inflation down -- likely to come under pressure the next policy tightening may have actually been brought forward a little."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"If they were going to cut rates it was always going to be sooner rather than later. There have been a few signs of softness in some of the recent indicators. They still seem to be fairly confident that the economy is picking up. And it really is the wages story that has driven this cut."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"I am certainly surprised at the timing but, put it this way, anyone who read their AFR (Australian Financial Review newspaper) this morning must have figured that it had to be a chance. That was a fairly good clue and of course it had quite an effect on the market this morning. It (the RBA's reasoning) is ok, I guess. It clearly isn't a risk free strategy."
